H1.text: A slow ball just taps your pads. A fast ball stings. A hammer swung hard drives a nail deep.

H2.text: Moving things carry something. Something that can push, hit and break.

H3.text: Aarav is at the college nets. A ball comes at ten metres per second. Just a tap on the pads.

H4.text: The next ball comes at twenty. Twice the speed. Does it hit twice as hard?

H5.text: No. It carries four times the energy. By the end of this video, you will see why.

P2.text: First, energy. Energy is the ability to do work: to push something through a distance.

P3.text: A moving hammer pushes a nail in. A moving ball pushes the pads back. Moving air turns a windmill.

P4.text: Each one does work, just because it is moving.

P5.text: The energy a body has because of its motion is called kinetic energy. Kinetic comes from a Greek word for motion. Its symbol is K.

S1.text: Let's build it on a live track.

S2.text: A two kilogram cart starts at rest. A steady four newton force pushes it, with no friction.

S3.text: After one metre, it moves at two metres per second. The force has done four joules of work.

S4.text: After four metres, the speed is four. The work is sixteen joules.

S5.text: After nine metres, the speed is six. Thirty six joules.

S6.text: Slow-mo replay of the first four metres.

S7.text: To double the speed, the same push had to act over four times the distance. So four times the work went in.

S8.text: Look at the graph. The stored work is the kinetic energy. It curves up, like v squared.

D1.text: Now the formula, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. A force F pushes a body from rest through a distance d. The work done is W equals F d.

D3.text: Step two. Newton's second law. F equals m a.

D4.text: Step three. Starting from rest, v squared equals two a d. So d equals v squared over two a.

D5.text: Step four. Put them together. W equals m a, times v squared over two a. The a cancels. W equals half m v squared.

D6.text: Step five. This work is stored in the motion. So kinetic energy K equals half m v squared, in joules.

D7.text: Step six. Momentum p equals m v. So K can also be written as p squared over two m.

T1.text: Remember this. Kinetic energy is half m v squared. Double the speed, and you get four times the energy.

C1.text: Now, mass or speed? Side by side.

C2.text: Double the mass, same speed. K doubles. Four joules become eight.

C3.text: Double the speed, same mass. K becomes four times. Four joules become sixteen.

C4.text: Now you try. One kilogram at six metres per second, or two kilograms at three. Which has more kinetic energy? Pause and decide.

C5.text: The light, fast ball! Eighteen joules against nine, because the speed is squared.

R1.text: Can kinetic energy ever be negative? Follow the links.

R3.text: Two. v squared is never negative, whichever way the body moves.

R4.text: Three. So K is never negative. It has no direction. It is a scalar.

K1.text: One more. A ball's velocity flips from plus four to minus four metres per second. Does its kinetic energy change? Pause and think.

K2.text: No! The speed is still four. Its momentum flipped, but its kinetic energy stayed the same.

W2.text: A cricket ball of zero point one six kilograms is bowled at twenty metres per second. Find its kinetic energy, and the speed at which it has a quarter of that.

W3.text: K equals half m v squared. Half, times zero point one six, times twenty squared.

W4.text: Twenty squared is four hundred. Zero point zero eight times four hundred is thirty two joules.

W5.text: A quarter of thirty two is eight joules. K is a quarter, so v squared is a quarter, and v is half.

W6.text: Ten metres per second. Aarav's slow ball: half the speed, a quarter of the energy.

X2.text: Many students think two bodies with the same momentum have the same kinetic energy.

X3.text: But K equals p squared over two m. For the same momentum, the lighter body has more kinetic energy.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In quick ratio and percentage questions linking K, mass, speed and momentum.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A trolley's momentum increases by fifty percent, with the same mass. By what percentage does its kinetic energy increase? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. One hundred and twenty five percent.

A2.text: K equals p squared over two m. With the same mass, K follows p squared.

A3.text: The new p is one point five p, so the new K is two point two five times K.

A4.text: The increase is one point two five K. One hundred and twenty five percent.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does a ball at twice the speed carry four times the energy?

Y3.text: Two. Can kinetic energy ever be negative?

Y4.text: Three. Two bodies have the same momentum. Which one has more kinetic energy?

N1.text: Next time: a bike going twice as fast needs four times the distance to stop. Why? We find out in the work-energy theorem.
